overview: These **243 simulated interviews** span the complete balanced archetype grid; they are constructed cases, not survey responses or population estimates.
In the dated AGI scenarios, **thinking AI** reaches contact-centre calls before capable robots reach physical work roughly three years later.
In the 2028 case, **199 of 243** are alarmed or panicked; posted paid work and household bills condition their plans.

S0.headline: Most contact-centre work continues in AI Plateau, while bills, targets and small software errors still matter.

whatTheyDo.text: Karl Usman keeps handling delivery complaints and checks original order dates by hand.
Carlos Ito tries to put fifty a month into savings for the first time.
Sara Bauer skips two paid Sunday market lunches monthly and puts their cost into the rent account.
Beth Larsen attends union canteen meetings to push back on call-time targets.

whatTheySay: **Original records** still need checking before an agent promises a delivery, refund or payment correction.
**Paid hours and targets** matter even when software saves only a little time.
whatTheyThink: **Current work** looks steady for many, especially where calls still need human correction.
**Rent and household wages** remain fragile for workers with little saved or variable partner income.
**Management choices** can raise call targets or cut shifts without a radical AI breakthrough.
howTheyFeel: **Calm** describes 124 of these 243 simulated profiles, whose work and money generally look steady.
**Anxious** describes 67, often because rent, low pay or variable household wages already threaten the budget.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.80 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.07 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The save-more action appears for 65 of 81 midlife profiles, versus 30 of 81 late-life profiles in these 243 simulations.

quotes.name: Karl Usman
quotes.text: A quiet AI year still has a rent date every month.

quotes.name: Sara Bauer
quotes.text: A receipt printed from the wrong line is still the wrong answer.

quotes.name: Hana Reyes
quotes.text: The customer’s stove does not get warmer because a message is tidier.

least.name: Buffered calm
least.story: All 124 calm profiles have moderate or strong savings; 75 have strong cushions, making ordinary disruptions easier to absorb.

most.name: Rent exposed
most.story: Of the 67 anxious profiles, 65 have thin savings; ordinary wage gaps and bills remain urgent even in AI Plateau.

thoughts.text: I expect my calls or pay to continue through modest change.
Household income and bills stay on my mind.
Savings or stable pay provide room, but need protecting.
Employer targets, contracts, or staffing remain a threat.
Small automation could alter calls, checks, or service quality.
My skills, tool use, or other plans still matter.

S1.headline: Steady Disruption moves routine calls to software, pushing agents to test tools and protect paid weekly work.

whatTheyDo.text: Karl Quinn applies after cuts only for posted paid reception with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after fare, first-bus access, and a signed offer before leaving.
Sara Bauer tests twelve old wrong transfers on paid time only if her supervisor permits error logging.
Bianca Garcia joins agents’ written demand for paid human appeal hours.
Tomas Petrov takes employer-funded training on paid time only if a posted paid audit role requires it.

whatTheySay: **Written paid hours** should show what remains when simple calls and chats move to software.
**Human correction** still needs time and authority when an automated answer is wrong.
**Real openings** matter more than promises of a new title or course.
whatTheyThink: **Routine queues** may shrink before many junior agents master harder cases.
**Experienced agents** may keep disputes, yet lose paid shifts or premiums as teams get smaller.
**Household budgets** depend on whole-week wages; nearby centres may face the same cuts.
howTheyFeel: **Anxious** describes 211 of 243 simulated profiles as their own paid work could realistically shrink.
**Alarmed** describes 20, mostly with thin savings and an expected near-term loss of calls or income.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.21 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.90 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The change-job action appears for 80 of 81 midlife profiles, versus 59 of 81 early-career profiles in these 243 simulations.

quotes.name: Karl Quinn
quotes.text: A job that starts before the first bus is no job I can hold.

quotes.name: Adam Larsen
quotes.text: I like testing a tool; I do not like a shorter pay packet.

quotes.name: Sara Bauer
quotes.text: An answer can be fast and still send a customer back to the wrong bill.

least.name: Room to adapt
least.story: All 12 calm or uneasy profiles are early-career; nine are adaptive and seven have strong savings in these simulations.

most.name: Cuts without buffer
most.story: Among 20 alarmed profiles, 17 have thin savings and 14 resist new tools as routine calls shrink.

thoughts.text: Software pressure threatens routine work, staffing, or the employer.
My paid hours or shift premium could fall.
Experience or learning may help with harder or technical work.
Household wages, bills, and savings shape the impact of a cut.
Nearby work or new roles may be uncertain or pay less.
Technical, hands-on, or independent work may offer another path.

S2.headline: In this simulated set of 243 call centre workers, 2028 AGI prompts immediate plans for lost screen work and household income.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Costa applies for supermarket, care home and bus depot cleaning jobs.
Nora Garcia cancels the extra television package if household income falls.
Victor Rahman asks his father about one mortgage payment only if due before another wage, after checking the shortfall and his ability to help.
Adam Garcia joins agents seeking written staffing dates and paid appeals with correction authority.
Adam Larsen charges for booked Saturday repairs and records receipts before buying more tools.

whatTheySay: **Thinking work** could go before the later robots touch physical jobs.
**Written dates** and **paid openings** matter more than a reassuring job title.
A short **cash reserve** cannot support a long unpaid course or search.
whatTheyThink: **Hands-on work** may buy time only until robots arrive about three years later.
**Savings** buy a search window, while a partner’s wage may not carry rent or mortgage alone.
Nearby centres and other **screen jobs** may cut at the same time.
howTheyFeel: **Alarmed** is the most common recorded mood: 191 of 243.
Another 44 are **anxious**, and 8 are **panicked**; none are recorded as calm or uneasy.

differences.text: Average worry is 4.09 among 81 with thin cushions versus 3.53 among 81 with strong cushions (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 4.00 among 81 resistant workers versus 3.70 among 81 adaptive workers (1 calm to 5 panicked).

quotes.name: Bianca Costa
quotes.text: If every thinking job goes in 2028, then the council office goes too, and robots don't take the shelf-stacking jobs until about 2031.

quotes.name: Victor Rahman
quotes.text: My wife's sewing income cannot carry the mortgage and two children alone, and our savings are under one month.

quotes.name: Victor Alvarez
quotes.text: Four months in a savings account is a bridge to another pay packet, not a second career.

thoughts.text: I see hands-on work as a possible bridge before later robots.
I know later robots do not protect my headset work.
I worry family income or housing cannot absorb my lost wage.
I cannot count on other work as a secure fallback.
I weigh what my savings can cover or let me try.
My present job or skill advantage may not last.

least.story: All 44 least worried are anxious; 38 have strong cushions, and 24 are adaptive.

most.name: Panicked with little cash
most.story: All eight most worried are panicked and resistant; seven have thin cushions.

S3.headline: In this simulated set of 243 call centre workers, 2031 AGI gives some time to learn or test work while wages last.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Costa takes the free two-evening care certificate at the local college.
Beth Larsen keeps working Northgate’s late shift while studying.
Erik Usman joins the staff request for paid review training tied to a posted vacancy.
Victor Alvarez tries a paid unloading shift only if offered and safe lifting is possible.
Adam Larsen logs repair hours and parts; adds a second Saturday slot only after receipts replace one lost shift’s pay for three straight months, keeping one rest day.

whatTheySay: **Five years** offers time to train, inspect paid roles and build a reserve.
Some **course plans** depend on real vacancies, funded fees or paid study time when household money is tight.
A new **review desk** can also face AGI; hands-on work faces robots around 2034.
whatTheyThink: Some can **learn or test** another route before the present desk shrinks.
A hands-on role may be a **bridge**, and another screen role may also face AGI.
**Paid hours** and **real openings** must be checked before treating a new route as household income.
howTheyFeel: **Anxious** is the most common recorded mood: 200 of 243.
Thirty are **uneasy** and 13 are **alarmed**; none are recorded as panicked or calm.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.07 among 81 with thin cushions versus 2.72 among 81 with strong cushions (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 3.10 among 81 resistant workers versus 2.78 among 81 adaptive workers (1 calm to 5 panicked).

quotes.name: Victor Kowalski
quotes.text: One paid site visit tells me more about my knees than a job title does.

quotes.name: Victor Rahman
quotes.text: Lifting stock for a neighbour once is not the same as being paid all week.

quotes.name: Victor Alvarez
quotes.text: A course earns its place only when a paid shift waits on the other side.

thoughts.text: I could use the extra years to build skills or explore work options.
The extra warning does not make my work safe.
I may waste the longer warning and remain unready.
Later robots may limit a hands-on path I consider.
Thinking AI may also affect work I hope to keep or enter.
Income, learning costs or real openings shape my preparation.

least.story: All 30 least worried are uneasy; 24 have strong cushions, and 18 are adaptive.

most.story: All 13 most worried are alarmed; 12 are resistant and eight have thin cushions.

S4.headline: A decade gives contact-centre workers room to prepare, but thinking AI can change desk jobs before later robots reach physical work.

whatTheyDo.text: Bianca Costa stays on the phones while watching colleagues try the care course first.
Priya Chen plans to learn upholstery and might build a small furniture repair service.
Gareth Ziegler plans monthly paid complaints practice if approved while keeping his call wage.
Omar Santos saves from his lead shift toward a full year, keeping a nine-month floor before a risky move.
Dana Patel would accept post-cut work only if weekly pay covers rent and travel with compatible start times.

whatTheySay: **A decade of warning** gives some people room to train, save or plan a move while still earning.
**Real paid work** matters more than a future job title when households must meet rent or mortgage payments.
**Calls change first** under thinking AI; later robots may also affect a physical-work fallback.
whatTheyThink: **Delay is a risk** for workers who know a distant deadline could let them drift.
**A new path** feels possible to some, while others doubt their current desk or a hands-on fallback will last.
**Retirement income** cannot be assumed from savings balances or a calendar date.
howTheyFeel: **Uneasy** is the most common mood: 138 of 243 profiles, alongside 81 anxious, 22 calm and 2 alarmed.
**Thin reserves** keep the long horizon uncomfortable where current rent or mortgage payments already press.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.85 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.85 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
The retrain action appears for 47 of 81 early-career profiles, versus 0 of 81 late-life profiles.

quotes.name: Marco Schmidt
quotes.text: Nobody really knows what 2036 looks like, and anybody who says they do is selling a course.

quotes.name: Hana Moreau
quotes.text: I can watch a decade of rotas without quitting a good wage today.

quotes.name: Dana Patel
quotes.text: Ten years is no answer to a rent bill due next week.

thoughts.text: A long warning can make me delay action.
The decade gives me time or options.
My wages, savings and housing costs still shape choices.
Thinking AI may still take my desk work.
Later robots also affect my plans.
I need verified income before planning later life.

least.name: Savings and options
least.story: Of 22 calm profiles, 15 have strong savings and 14 are adaptive; 14 are early-career, often with time to build another route.

most.name: Thin cash buffers
most.story: Of 83 anxious or alarmed profiles, 67 have thin savings; rent and mortgage pressure persists despite a decade to prepare.
